title: Our Embodied Life, Part 4: Resiliancy and Chiyono's No Moon, No Water
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach closes the Our Embodied Life series by reading the story of Chiyono, a servant whose patched bucket gives way under a full moon, and her poem "Where water does not collect, the moon does not dwell." Ryushin names resiliency as the thread through the month's stories, pairing effort with pliancy alongside Mahapajapati's fearlessness and Kisa Gotami's compassion. Examples include a student who sat a whole sesshin with an abscessed tooth and Alan Senauke's teacher telling him, as a young jikido fussing over cushions, "Just let it fall apart." Sangha members then share their own patched buckets, including a memory of women in Africa carrying water on their heads.

sentences.text: **Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Good evening everyone.
Welcome to some of the new faces that I haven't seen here before and welcome particularly to our spiritual guiding teacher here.
Welcome back, Tim.
So this marks the last of our series of teachings on our embodied life, and I really appreciate everyone's attention.
Not too many people have run away.
What I hope to do with this evening is make some kind of concluding and inclusive remarks on all the topics that we've talked about.

I'm not going to, I hope I'm not going to speak all that long because we're going to end a little early tonight for a special ceremony, followed by a little bit of a farewell for one of our sangha members who's moving on to the East Coast.

I'd like to leave time hopefully for us to see what's been percolating for you in this last month in terms of some of the topics that we've talked about, about how we embody practice out of our lives in a day-to-day way.

As you know, those of you who've been able to attend, I've been speaking in part out of a response to what's happening in the world events, and I find that that continues to touch me very, very deeply.
As I was drafting this talk last weekend, I opened my iPhone up and heard about yet another series of shootings in Munich.
As I was getting ready to prepare to come over here, the New York Times posted a review of 247 people who had died in a two-week period in terrorist attacks around the world at the end of March.

We're surrounded by examples of leadership and response that can seem intolerant, fragile, unstable, unable to bear dissent or perceive threat—the kind of fragility that seems to be due to a certain view of the self and of the world.
I know that place in myself.

My goodness, I've spent a lot of time and energy, particularly in my younger years, in overly attentive analysis of what I did wrong and how I could be better: a fragile self, thrown out of balance for the conflict from within myself, actually not from without, although it's not always apparent to ourselves when it is.
I was thinking about all this and I was considering, well, what's the response?
We come to practice, and I think in difficult times, either in our personal lives or in our world circumstance, we look to say, "How am I guided by this in my practice?
Where is the grounding here for a life bigger than my own?"
I was thinking back on all the different stories that we've talked about and reflected on this month, and the word that came to my mind is resiliency.

How do we have find our own internal resiliency, our own backbone and sense of self and strength about what to do at a time when we feel pretty jostled around by the events and the emotions and the stories that come up?

The definition of resiliency is an ability to recover from and adjust easily to misfortune or change, the capacity of a strained body to recover its size and shape after deformation caused by compressive stress, the ability to recover readily from illness, depression, adversity or the like.
It turns out in Buddhism that buoyancy or pliancy is another term, and it is one of the eleven virtuous mental faculties.
We don't talk very much about pliancy.
It gets paired sometimes with effort.
Effort has a certain amount of directiveness and trying that can tip over to straining that has too much purposefulness.
Buoyancy or pliancy is a willingness to accommodate, to settle back, to be flexible, and so those two factors get paired, each helping the other.
Too much pliancy or buoyancy has no directedness, and too much effort misses what's actually happening, as we will review a bit tonight in the story of Chiyono, No Water, No Moon.

I think as I was reflecting on what these stories we've read and really what was underneath some of what I was attempting to talk about, what we were talking about, it's pointing all in the same direction of this quality of resiliency and where that arises from out of our practice lives.
We talked about Mahapajapati's fearlessness; it is a response to our own truth, not a truth of opinion or views or ideas, but that which is our real essence, our true self.
That was her fearlessness.
We talked about the deep acceptance and the compassion that arose in Kiso Togami as she accepted the unthinkable and the unbearable.
She was only able to do this because she understood everyone shared her pain, and so she had the capacity to bear it not just her own, but everyone else's on a deeper level than she ever had before.

And it's Senjo knowing herself so well and accepting herself so completely that she didn't need to be anyone in particular; that we don't need to be any one particular fixed to any idea or sense of self.
With that, we have an improvisational fluidity, appliances and flexibility with how we live our lives.

So this talk, this call on the story could be from many different orientations, but I invite you to consider the qualities of appliances or resiliency as we read the story tonight, and I make a few comments.
I was interested to know that Chiyono, her other name was Mugai Nyodai, who if you chant the women's lineage anywhere, you've had the opportunity to do that, you know that she's one of our ancestors.
She was the first woman in Japan to actually be recognized as a teacher.
She was in the Rinzai lineage, but she was a recognized Sen teacher.
She had her beginnings perhaps in the story.
The historical Mugai Nyodai may have been a slightly different person; apparently that woman was highly educated and the daughter of a samurai.
The story is told a little bit differently.
Let's read it.
I think it only has five paragraphs, so maybe we can go around.
Whoever has the story handy will go down maybe this side first since we did the opposite side last time, and start with you, John, and anyone who has it, the next person who has it can just move.
You ready?
**Participant:** Chiyono was a servant in a Zen convent who wanted to practice zazen.
One day she approached an elderly nun and asked, "I'm of humble birth.
I can't read or write and must work all the time.
Is there any possibility that I could attain the way of Buddha even though I have no skills?"
The nun answered her, "This is wonderful, my dear.
In Buddhism, there are no distinctions between people.
There is only this: each person must hold fast to the desire to awaken and cultivate a heart of great compassion.
People are complete as they are.
If you don't fall into the lucid thoughts, there is no Buddha and no sentient being.
There is only one complete nature.
If you want to know your true nature, you need to turn toward the source of your lucid thoughts.
This is called zazen."
Chiyono said with happiness, "With this practice as my companion, I have only to go about my daily life practicing day and night."
After months of wholehearted practice, she went out on a full moon night to draw some water from the well.
The bottom of her old bucket held together by bamboo strips suddenly gave way, and the reflection of the moon matched with the water.
When she saw this, she attained great realization.
Her enlightenment poem was this:
*With this and that, I tried to keep the bucket together and then the bottom fell out.
Where water does not collect, the moon does not grow.*
Marla Kodunboi's reflection for several years now.
We'll stop now.
Thank you.
So in this story, she's only a poor girl.
She doesn't have any great ideas; she's just making an everyday effort doing what there is to do in her routines.
She's continually holding, I'd say, her trust.
Wasn't that remarkable what she says?
"With practice as my guide, all I need to do is keep showing up."
So with great trust, she wholeheartedly applies herself to looking at her delusive thinking in whatever way that is.
One night she's carrying her bucket to the well; the moon she's looking to carry is in it.
The moon being, as many of us know, the symbol of enlightenment.
This is the this and that of her enlightenment poem.
It's running after this and that, running after enlightenment.
Her well-intended intention to wake up is a kind of this and that.
That's the effort we make, the this and that, to try and keep ourselves together.
Whether it's our successes in school or work, finding the right relationship, whatever it is in life or just keeping up, we're always running after this and that.
Or it might be in the forms: "Am I getting it right?
Am I cutting the flowers exactly right for the altar?
Am I brushing the zavutas correctly?
Am I practicing right?
Am I doing right?"
My zazen doesn't seem to be going anywhere.
Somehow we have the idea that we can keep it all together, and if we keep it all together, that somehow we'll realize something, we'll have the life that we want to have.
On some level, I think we come to practice in part because we want to wake up, right?
We want the moon that's in the bucket; we want enlightenment.
Maybe there's nothing really wrong with that, but at some point the wanting and the going after is actually an impediment.
We want to be good enough.
We want to be good enough, and we think if we come to practice we might be.
So there's a kind of an exhaustion that comes, arises out of that, a kind of emotional exhaustion, as if we're trying to keep some idea of ourself together, who we should be.
I've seen many an elderly, usually woman, who insists on doing her housework, even though doing it she becomes so low on oxygen that she passes out, collapses, almost dies.
Or the young Zen, I have a dear friend, as a committed young Zen student who sat with an abscessed tooth through all of a sesshin because that was being a good student.
That's trying to hold it all together.
Close on Alan Sinaki, who's the vice avid at Berkeley, likes to tell a story on himself.
One of his first positions when he came to the Berkeley Zendo was being the Jikido.

Jikido is the one who cleans the temple, so he was responsible for making sure someone was brushing off all the cushions, arranging them just so, two hand breasts apart from each other, that everything was tidied exactly as so.
And that was a long time ago.
Alan was both really anxious and really intent on having it done right.
And so his teacher said to him, "Just let it fall apart, just let it fall apart."
Practicing with letting things fall apart means not the way I want it done, not directing others to do just so, not being too anxious or too bossy, but allowing things to be as they are.
My first teacher used to call it leading from behind, seeing what's needed and responding to it.
What comes up when we let things fall apart?
What do we notice about ourselves?

What do we notice about the space that we create for other people to come forward and express themselves, to be themselves, to interact with each other and make something happen when we allow things to fall apart, when we allow ourselves not to know how it needs to be this or that.
In her commentary, Sensei Meryl Boyd says, "We're called to awareness instead of vigilance."
What a relief to be free of that vigilance.
So what's the moon in the bucket, right?
This enlightenment, our ideal self, a place we can reside and rest without worry.
It's freedom; it's the freedom we give ourselves.
We talk about the finger pointing at the moon, but both the words and the efforts to lead us to enlightenment and indeed the very idea we have about it are just encouragements.
They're just encouragements when they aren't impediments, when our ideas about them don't get in our way.
And over time, practicing this way, the old ties weaken.
The old ties of ourselves to our ideas of ourselves and ideas weaken and the bottom drops out.
There is no perfect self.
There's no trying to get there.
We miss out on our lives as they're happening.
We're called to awareness instead of vigilance, just actually being in our life with nonjudgmental complete presence and fluidity to respond.
I might say we're called to confidence or trust in our lives instead of worry or fear or striving.
Perhaps it's a leap for you, but consider it.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** The enlightenment poem she wrote said, "With this and that, I tried to keep the bucket together.
And then the bottom fell out.
Where water does not collect, the moon does not dwell."
The water is like the ocean and the waves, the ocean of the entirety of life, and the waves are manifestations on it.
This vast life and all the movement of the mind and the activity, life keeps flowing—not a thing, but a continually shifting activity.
What is it when the water falls out?
Of course, Chiano made an effort, an everyday wholehearted effort.
It is unlikely this would have happened if she hadn't.
Effort in and of itself is not delusional, but it understands its function and uses the function instead of being used by it.

Sensei Boyd says again in her commentary, "Ironically, it is precisely that conditioning of keeping it all together that gave me, an African-American woman, the courage to walk into a Zen center for the first time."

I had been trained to tolerate the circumstance of being other, to maintain a public identity in places where I was allowed, but not possibly welcome, like the schools and the libraries of my childhood.
Zen centers offered something that I deeply needed: a place to experience my life in the world more deeply.
I hoped I would be welcome at a Zen center, and I also knew it could be otherwise.
This is her fearlessness—to walk into this uncertainty, I relied on being outwardly upright while keenly aware of inner fears.

As Zen students, we live between Gionno's first two lines, "With this and that, I tried to keep the bucket together, and then the bottom fell out," and the second two lines, "Where water does not collect, the moon, our ideas of ourselves, of enlightenment, does not dwell."
Letting them fall apart, knowing how to keep things together, is a valuable skill.
It was knowing how to care for things that led Gionno to continually patch the bucket.
When it fell apart, she made excellent use of that circumstance as well.
Our liberation depends and deepens with the refinement of our capacity for flexibility and discernment: resiliency, clientsy, and wisdom.
I would say, "Where the water does not collect, the moon does not dwell, surrender your life," or trust that your life in this moment is exactly right.
It is not a hair out of place to the moment, and go with it.
Go with it means trust it.
The moon does not dwell means no place to land, no place to go.
This is perfect clientsy and complete wisdom, Mahapajapati's fearlessness, and Kisa Togami's unbounded compassion.
So that is what I have to say tonight.
I wonder what you have to say tonight.

What is your response, your reaction, what comes up for you around anything that has been on your mind, related to practice, how we have been talking, what has happened in the world, and your response to it.
I do not have anything to say except I appreciate your reading us these stories very much.
Thank you.
Thank you, Judy.
The night that you talked about, what is her name, Kisa Togami, probably some of you noticed that I sat on the cushion and cried the whole evening.
And that is because I have a special needs son, so I do not have a child who died.
But I guess my idea, we like to have a child, has just died over and over again.
So that has been hard.
So I thought I would just let you know why I am just sitting here crying.
It strikes me that all these stories respond to what is really going on.
For me, I want to run off into my imagination all the time.
The worse the news, the faster I want to run off into some imaginary way for that not to be true.
It is so harsh sometimes and difficult.
It reminds me of too many things in my own life.
I want to take off fast and get into some kind of imaginary response.
It is really hard to sit with it.
It has been my practice from here on out, trying to stay with what is really going on instead of what I would like to be going on or what I cannot imagine should be going on in any of these stories.
I think your broken heart, your broken heart is your response.
That is what allows you to turn towards...
Discussion has come up in a few Dharma talks elsewhere about the koans that are part of the personality of the group, the koans that we come back to.
As an everyday Zen community, the story of sento just feels like that.
Trying to keep things together is strongly a dramatic way of practice.
I am wondering if this will be one that comes up again and again.

Part of what stands out about that koan for me, and the reason it was important to me that she was a poor servant, is that she was running around doing this and that as a lay person, trying to keep her life together.
What comes up for you?
How is it emblematic of your lay life?
Well, it does seem to be that the go-to place the intention is not fully present but is working toward putting things right, sewing the bucket up.
Oh, jeez, I am sewing the bucket up again.
Oh yeah, okay.
Yeah, what does it mean to sew the bucket up with this mind when you are in charge and responsible?
Yes, please.
I just wanted to highlight that her willingness to do the work and to carry the water.
I have just been somewhere where today, women are carrying the water on their heads for their families.
You have to do that every day.
You cannot turn on the tap.
So this story, using what she had available, whether it is an old bucket.
In Africa, where I was, it was like a sort of yellow, I guess we called them jerry canes actually, from the British.
I do not know how many gallons they held, quite a few.
It is so big.
You want to have one or it is nice, two on your head.
Walking along, walking along.
So there is willingness to just do what has to be done.
These women know what pipes are, and they know that they do not have that.
They do not know what things are like in that time in Japan.
So that willingness to just keep going.
That is a part of this for me.
I think that willingness to just keep going.
Maybe things fell apart today, maybe they do not, but we just keep going.
That sounds like Raising Nathaniel.
Yes.
What comes up for me is like a conundrum, because I find that for myself, I have a tendency toward slop and torpor, so I feel like I have to make myself keep going.
And yet, I understand the certain fruitlessness of people constantly trying to make things happen to the way they want them to be.
But it seems like there is a place where you have to find, it is just that energy that you just discussed where there is resilience versus effortfulness.
That is right.
You cannot fall too deeply into resilience or strive too far into it.
In all of these examples, the key point is the pliancy behind the effort.
So you have to keep going.
You have to keep responding.
You have to keep getting up and making an effort.
Where are you going?
What are you doing?
What is the reasoning behind it?
Are you trying to do it in a particular way?
Are you doing it for what reasoning are you doing it?
You are taking care of your child.
You are providing for your family.
You are getting yourself up to respond to what you need to do with your life and making that effort.
Nothing more than that.
And whatever comes up, the jar falls off your head.
It is broken.
You keep going.
Another disaster, another illness, another unpredicted experience, you just respond to it.
You do not want to get up.
My teacher always said, you set the alarm and you get up.
You do not think about sitting zazen.
You set the alarm and you get up, and you just come and sit.
Period.
It is that effort.
It is not about wanting to be seen.
I showed up at zazen or whatever.
You are just showing up and doing the next thing.
You talked about a relief when you finally just let it go.
I have found repeatedly as that family goes through the catastrophe of a person having an illness and trying to put the bottom into the bucket for a long time, it does not work.
But to sit down at one question has become this greatest opportunity to move forward, to move forward.
That talk tonight really kind of spoke to my practice of what I felt like.
I feel my deepest longing is that just really letting go completely.
I never heard this story before.
I heard that metaphor of the bottom of the bucket falling on your voice.
I just longed for that.
That is all I had to say.
I was disappointed that I missed the first few weeks of the seminar.
And then I came tonight and I was really looking forward to it.
And I am sitting back here and I am feeling my age.
I could not hear a thing.
I am so sorry I did not ask if everyone could hear.
It is okay.
It is really putting me in touch with what I have been going through, some physical changes, and I can feel the senses declining.
So I guess through the whole process I had an opportunity to feel that whole loss.

And then I began to be concerned because it seemed so much a part of the Dharma to be able to be with your senses and to be there and to be present and feeling like I am losing them or the capacity of my body.
It is just a grief feeling.
How do I still stay present and be in it here when part of me is not?
Well, I think part of it is that you sit closer so you can hear.
No, I am really, yeah.
And the senses that are more accessible you experience them more fully.
A blind person can see.
A blind person sees in other ways.
That is letting the bottom of the bucket drop out.
That is letting the bottom of the bucket drop out.

I have been thinking a lot about what we talked about yesterday or I am sorry, last week about the multiple outfits we can wear and uniforms we can wear throughout our lives and how we kind of embody these things.

I have been in a form in my life recently, just graduated from college and kind of trying out all these different uniforms and realizing that whatever I choose is going to be what I have become and who I am.
Realizing that has made the weight of that decision paralyzing in a way.
So my practice has been a lot of thinking about how I can kind of let all those anxieties and expectations about my ideal self drop away and be present.
So now in the present, untangle all of that.
Have curiosity.
Have curiosity.
Whatever you wind up doing next is an exploration.
It will be changing and moving.
That is not the role.
It is just a role.
It is not the self.
Have curiosity about what that is.
I think we are almost out of time.
I do not know if anyone has anything that they would like to be sure.
I see you often in the face.
I look at you very often.

But I really felt called to share because this idea of putting the bottom of your bucket all up has just really become clear to me, especially in my own personal life, the deckings of just my entire lifetime and whether I have an illness or not an illness, and of recognizing this innate desire to always want to fix the bucket, want to just do my part to help the family and to keep things together.

But realizing now just kind of letting the bucket fall out and just the idea of really understanding this sense of still caring and loving and letting things be and accepting that this is what is really helping me in my personal life and my resilience and my attempt to really find a place where I can still love my mom conditionally and be there for the family but not feel as suffering.
For so long this kind of need to fix the bucket or just kind of keep things in place.
See what there was that I could do to help cause so much suffering in my life too because of all of these stories that I told myself.
Just kind of if I do this, it will make it better.
If I do these things, it will make it better too.
So yeah, I just really appreciate it.
Thank you very much for your practice.
